newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian leftist head campaigns to change image.
newsitem.headline: Albanian leftist head campaigns to change image.

text.p: Albanian Socialist leader Fatos Nano, campaigning hard in a general election three months after his release from prison, is probably Albania's only politician capable of making a serious challenge for the presidency.
Nano heads a party carrying the difficult legacy of Albania's hardline communists, who ruled Albania for 45 years under paranoid leader Enver Hoxha.
The Socialists officially shed the Marxist label of their predecessors last year and Nano has spent much of the campaign stressing his credentials as a defender of the market.
"Like you, we want free enterprise and private property," he told a rally in the closing stages of the campaign. "It is our historic obligation to make Albania part of Europe."
He tells voters the election is their chance to rid Albania of the authoritian rule of President Sali Berisha.
Nano, 45, was among the first Albanian thinkers to publish articles questioning the orthodoxies of one-party rule and a centralised economy, in 1990 before the collapse of communism.

He was prime minister twice -- at the head of Albania's last communist administration in 1991 and after the first multi-party elections won by the Socialists. But his term ended within weeks when he was forced out by a general strike.
Nano was jailed for 12 years in 1994 after being implicated in an Italian aid scandal and international human rights groups campaigned for his release.

Pardoned by Berisha and released in March at the height of the revolt gripping Albania, Nano initially said Berisha should quit. But now he urges the president to work with the Socialist majority he says is certain to emerge from the election.
"I feel younger and more accepted by younger people," he said recently of how he has felt since his release. "I've already forgotten that I lost four years of my life."

Many Albanians believe Nano could become a rallying point for the country, divided into a south controlled by armed rebels demanding Berisha's resignation and the north where law and order is shaky after similar mass looting of weapons.
Seven years after the fall of communism, Nano is working out a credo, torn between two European Socialist prime ministers -- France's Lionel Jospin and Britain's Tony Blair.
"The philosophy of privatisation, social assistance, denationalisation and decentralisation of power is the future of my country," he said.
"Jospin said 'We will modernise the left' and Blair said 'We want to move the left to the centre quickly.' So I found myself in between. But my English is as good as my French."

Nano himself is untainted by the scandal over the failure of the pyramid savings schemes that bankrupted thousands of families, as he was in jail when they flourished. Rebels in the south accuse Berisha of not warning people of the risks.
Fatos Nano was born in Tirana on September 16, 1952 -- his father was a journalist who became head of state Radio and TV -- and studied political economics at Tirana University.

After three years as an economist at a steel works in central Albania, he returned to Tirana to work in the Institute of Marxist-Leninist studies, a think-tank led by Hoxha's widow and worked part-time as an economist and economy professor.

When communist rule ended Nano became secretary-general of the cabinet, deputy prime minister and then premier. Nano speaks English, French and Italian and knows several Slav languages. He is married with two teenage children.
